claims.text: A Pulumi package is the unit of versioning and distribution.
Components inside a Pulumi package inherit the package's version.
Pulumi packages come in two flavors (source-based and executable-based), and each is versioned and released differently.
A source-based plugin package is distributed as source code in a Git repository.
A source-based Pulumi package's version is the Git tag on its repository.
Publishing a source-based Pulumi package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry is a two-step flow, typically performed by a CI/CD pipeline that runs on tag.
The first step of publishing a source-based package to the Private Registry is applying a semver Git tag (for example, `v1.2.3`) to the repository.

The second step of publishing a source-based package to the Private Registry is running `pulumi package publish` to send the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and place the package in the Private Registry.
The `pulumi package publish` step often runs automated tests before publishing.
Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing a source-based package to the Private Registry.
Source-based packages referenced directly from a `Pulumi.yaml` file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.

An executable-based plugin package is distributed as a pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds such as npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, the Go module proxy, or private equivalents.
An executable-based Pulumi package's version is the version embedded in the published binary and SDKs.
Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.
Releases of executable-based packages are produced by a CI/CD pipeline that builds the plugin, generates the SDKs, and pushes everything to the relevant feeds.
In both the source-based and executable-based cases, the released artifact is a single, semantically-versioned Pulumi package.
Pulumi recommends that a repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package, regardless of package type.

A repository containing multiple Pulumi packages must either release them in lockstep, forcing unrelated work to share a version, or invent per-package release tooling that fights the way Pulumi naturally consumes packages.
Multiple components inside a single Pulumi package are fine and expected, and ship together at the package's version.

Pulumi's recommended approach is to define exactly one package per repository, group a cohesive set of components together inside that package, and use multiple repositories — one per package — to manage the distinct packages an organization publishes.
The Amazon EKS package in the Pulumi Registry bundles a managed Kubernetes cluster component along with the supporting components needed to secure and operate it.
The components in the Amazon EKS Pulumi Registry package are almost always used together and tend to evolve together.
One `PulumiPlugin.yaml` file at the repository root defines a Pulumi package.
It is technically possible to use a single monorepo containing one giant package for all of an organization's components, but Pulumi does not recommend this approach.
Bundling many unrelated components into a single package forfeits meaningful semantic versioning, which is how consumers know whether a given change is a bug fix, a new feature, or a breaking change.
When unrelated components share a package, every release of the package versions every component the same way, regardless of whether each component changed, which violates semver.
In the walkthrough example, the package is released at v1.0.0 with both ComponentA and ComponentB at v1.0.0.
In the walkthrough example, an enhancement made only to ComponentA results in the package being released at v1.1.0, even though ComponentB is unchanged.
In the walkthrough example, a breaking change made only to ComponentB results in the package being released at v2.0.0, even though ComponentA had no change at all.
